title: The Dubious Science of Arson Investigation
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the history of arson investigation, which for decades relied on folklore and intuition rather than science. They cover early handbooks (1945 book by Harry Rethert, Paul Kirk's 1969 Fire Investigation), the 1970s federal push that created the Center for Fire Research and the cone calorimeter, flashover and backdraft science, the Oakland Hills fire (1991) and crazed glass, the 1986 DuPont Plaza Hotel fire, the 1990 Lime Street fire in Jacksonville and the recreation experiment, and the Cameron Todd Willingham case in Texas, which ended in execution in 2004. They discuss the ongoing resistance in the field, modern methods for finding fire origin (body evidence, arcing, ignitable liquids database), and recommend reading David Grann's New Yorker article and Douglas Starr's Discover piece. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about Habitat 67.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Birthday greetings to Chuck and Jerry, and Josh's account of seeing Bob Dylan in Athens, Georgia.

segments.title: Introduction to unscientific arson investigation
segments.summary: The hosts frame arson investigation as long based on folklore and intuition, with sources David Grann and Douglas Starr, and mention the film Backdraft.

segments.title: Early handbooks and the 1945 book
segments.summary: The first fire investigation book, published in 1945 by Harry Rethert, was aimed at law enforcement looking to prove arson. Paul Kirk's 1969 book pushed the scientific method, and the field said there was too little science to compare against.

segments.title: Folk indicators of arson
segments.summary: The hosts list traditional signs of arson: the most burned area as origin, charred floors, puddle-shaped char, V-shaped soot, and crazed glass, which were believed to indicate accelerants.

segments.title: Federal research and the cone calorimeter
segments.summary: After a 1973 government report on fire damage, the government funded the Center for Fire Research. Researchers developed the cone calorimeter for repeatable burn experiments and a database.

segments.title: Flashover and backdraft
segments.summary: Flashover is when smoke gases ignite and the room fully catches fire, around 1000 degrees Celsius. Flashover can produce burn marks that had been wrongly attributed to accelerants, and it is related to backdraft.

segments.title: Oakland Hills fire and crazed glass
segments.summary: The 1991 Oakland fire, which destroyed close to three thousand homes, showed that crazed glass results from water spray on hot glass, not arson.

segments.title: DuPont Plaza Hotel fire
segments.summary: The 1986 New Year's Eve fire at the DuPont Plaza Hotel in San Juan, Puerto Rico, killed about 98 people. Computer models built from calorimeter data confirmed witness accounts that disgruntled workers set furniture on fire.

segments.title: Lime Street fire and recreation experiment
segments.summary: In Jacksonville, Florida, in 1990, Gerald Lewis was charged after a fire killed his family members. Investigators John Lentini and John DeHaan helped, and a recreation of the house with about $20,000 spent showed the couch fire produced the supposed arson evidence.

segments.title: Slow adoption and the Daubert standard
segments.summary: Changes trickled down slowly. In 1997 the International Association of Arson Investigators argued against applying the Daubert standard, which required scientific method for expert testimony.

segments.title: NFPA 2011 assumption of arson
segments.summary: The hosts say the 2011 NFPA manual advised that if the cause could not be determined by elimination, investigators should assume arson.

segments.title: Cameron Todd Willingham case
segments.summary: In December 1991 in Corsicana, Texas, Cameron Willingham's house fire killed his three children. Fire investigators, including Manuel Vasquez, called it arson based on pour patterns and red flags such as an Iron Maiden poster. Willingham was executed in 2004. Gerald Hurst later demolished the evidence, but the Board of Pardons and Paroles upheld the conviction.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Overturning convictions and resistance to change
segments.summary: Overturning arson convictions is hard because evidence is often lost. NFPA 921 is the gold standard guide, aimed at insurers and law firms. Civil courts have become more savvy than criminal courts, and investigators have resisted change.

segments.title: Finding fire origin scientifically
segments.summary: Modern methods include studying victims' bodies (edema close to the fire versus carbon monoxide further away), and arc marks on wiring that show whether power was on. A flashover study found investigators were right about 84 percent of the time if the fire was put out within thirty seconds of flashover.

segments.title: Ignitable liquids database and first responder guidelines
segments.summary: The Ignitable Liquids Reference Collection database (ILRCD) can identify flammable liquids found at fire scenes. Guidelines help firefighters and EMS record useful details at the scene.

segments.title: Josh's childhood shed anecdote
segments.summary: Josh describes exploring an abandoned shed as a kid and being questioned by police about a suspected insurance fire. Chuck jokes about the anecdote, and Josh admits he made it up.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Chuck recommends reading David Grann's Trial by Fire and Douglas Starr's Discover article, then transitions to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Habitat 67
segments.summary: A listener from McGill shares a fun fact that architect Moshe Safdie used Lego blocks to model Habitat 67 and bought out Montreal toy stores' Legos. The listener is named Kestrel.
